opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the unit of evaluation is no longer a single answer. It's a whole trajectory. In the chat era, you could look at one response and ask whether it was good. With agents, the model is taking dozens or hundreds of steps: calling tools, reading results, recovering from mistakes, deciding when to stop. So the team has to change how it thinks about data, training, and evaluation all at once.

First, on data. Static, human-written demonstrations are much less sufficient now. What matters more is building environments where the model can actually act and get feedback, like real codebases, real browsers, and real tool APIs. A lot of the competitive advantage is moving from "who has the best corpus" to "who has the richest, most realistic environments and the best verifiers." If you can't check whether a long task was really completed, you can't do reinforcement learning on it reliably.

Second, on training. Reinforcement learning becomes central rather than a finishing touch. But long-horizon RL is hard. Credit assignment over many steps, reward hacking, and infrastructure for rollouts that may take minutes each are all problems. Teams need to invest seriously in systems engineering. The algorithm people and the infra people can't be separate worlds anymore. Rollout throughput, sandboxing, and asynchronous training pipelines are now research problems in their own right.

Third, the base model still matters a lot. Some people think agent capability is purely post-training, but in my experience, if the pretrained model doesn't have strong reasoning, long-context handling, and good world knowledge, RL just amplifies a weak foundation. So you have to co-design. Pretraining should anticipate what the agent will need, like code, structured interaction, and long documents, and post-training should be designed around what pretraining gives you.

Fourth, on evaluation. Benchmarks saturate quickly, and agent benchmarks are especially easy to overfit. I think teams should keep a set of internal tasks that look like real work, and actually watch the trajectories, not just the final score. You learn a lot from seeing where the model gets stuck, loops, or gives up too early.

Finally, organizationally, I'd say: stay small and focused, and let people own problems end to end. The agent paradigm moves very fast. A team that can quickly go from "we noticed this failure mode" to "we built an environment for it, trained on it, and verified the fix" will beat a much larger team that's split into rigid silos. Efficiency, both compute efficiency and iteration speed, matters more than raw scale for most teams.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the agent paradigm forces a pretty fundamental rethinking of what "model development" even means, and a lot of teams haven't internalized that yet.

In the chat era, the loop was simple: you pretrain, you do SFT and RL on single-turn or short multi-turn data, you evaluate on benchmarks, and the model is the product. Under the agent paradigm, the model is one component in a system that includes tools, memory, an environment, and a long horizon of actions where errors compound. So the first shift I'd push teams toward is this: stop optimizing the model in isolation. Optimize the model-plus-environment as a unit. That means your training signal has to come from real task completion in realistic environments, not from whether a single response looks good to a human rater.

Concretely, I'd say three things.

First, environments are the new data. In the old world, the scarce resource was high-quality text. Now the scarce resource is a diverse, verifiable, realistically messy set of environments where an agent can act, fail, and get a signal. Building those is unglamorous engineering work, but I think it's the main moat going forward. Teams that treat environment construction as a first-class research problem, rather than something you hack together for a demo, will pull ahead.

Second, you have to design for long-horizon reliability, not peak capability. An agent that is brilliant 95 percent of the time but hallucinates a tool call or loses track of state at step 40 is useless for real work, because the failure wipes out everything before it. So things like calibrated uncertainty, knowing when to stop and ask, recovering from a bad action, and keeping a coherent internal plan across a very long context matter more than another few points on a reasoning benchmark. A lot of this is about reward design in RL. If you only reward the final outcome, you get agents that take wild shortcuts. You need process-level signals too, and you need to be very careful about reward hacking, because agents are extremely good at finding holes in your verifier.

Third, the organization has to change along with the model. In the chat era, you could separate the research team from the product team fairly cleanly. With agents, the boundary dissolves. The people building the training environments need to understand what real users actually do with the agent, and the people deploying it need to feed failure cases back into training very quickly. The teams I've seen do this well run a tight loop: deploy, collect trajectories, identify the failure modes, turn them into environments or evals, train, redeploy. If that cycle takes months, you lose. It needs to be weeks or less.

One more thing I'd add, and it's maybe a little contrarian: don't over-rotate on scaffolding. There's a temptation, when the model isn't good enough, to compensate with elaborate orchestration, lots of hand-written prompts, rigid workflows. That works in the short term, but it's debt. Every time the base model gets better, that scaffolding becomes a ceiling instead of a floor. I'd rather push capability into the model through training and keep the scaffold thin and general. Let the model learn to plan, to use tools, to recover. The job of the team is to build the environment and the signal that teaches it, not to hard-code the behavior.

So if I had to summarize: treat environments as data, optimize for reliability over a long horizon, close the loop between deployment and training very fast, and resist the urge to paper over model weaknesses with scaffolding. That's roughly how I think about it.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point should be what we want the agent to accomplish, and then we work backward to the model. It’s not enough to ask whether the model can give a good answer in one turn. We need to ask whether it can carry out a task over many steps, use tools appropriately, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover.

That changes how a team develops models. Model training, the agent framework, and evaluation need a much tighter feedback loop. When an agent fails, is it because the model lacks a capability, because the tool interface is confusing, or because important context was lost? Those problems can look similar in the final result, but they need different solutions.

I would also put more emphasis on evaluating complete tasks. Can the agent finish the work reliably? How much human intervention does it need? How much time and computation does it consume? A stronger benchmark score is useful, but it doesn’t necessarily translate into a better agent.

So I’d encourage teams to build that end-to-end development loop early. Let real task failures guide the next training and system improvements, rather than treating the agent as something you add after the model is finished.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is to treat the model and the agent system as one development problem. We used to focus heavily on whether a model could produce a good answer in a single turn. With agents, we have to ask whether it can carry a task through: understand the goal, use tools, recognize mistakes, and recover when something goes wrong.

That changes the feedback loop. Teams need to study complete task trajectories, not just individual responses. If an agent fails, was the problem reasoning, missing information, tool use, or the way the environment was designed? Those failures should guide both model training and system improvements.

I would also bring model researchers, infrastructure engineers, and product teams much closer together. Start with real tasks, establish reliable evaluations, and iterate across the whole system. The important measure is whether the agent completes useful work reliably, with a reasonable amount of time, compute, and human intervention.
